concept.name: Value at risk
concept.definition: A quantile-based measure of portfolio loss: for a given confidence level and horizon, the loss level that will not be exceeded with that probability under stated assumptions — a one-day 95% VaR of $1M means a 5% chance of losing more than $1M in a day. Formalized at J.P. Morgan in the early 1990s and embedded in bank capital regulation by the 1996 Basel market-risk amendment.
concept.intuition: It compresses the whole loss distribution into one sentence: on 19 days out of 20, we expect to lose no more than this.
concept.mechanics: Estimated parametrically (variance-covariance), by historical simulation, or by Monte Carlo, over a fixed horizon (one day, ten days) and tail probability (1%, 5%). VaR systems are validated by backtesting: the long-run frequency of breaches — losses beyond VaR — should match the specified tail probability.
concept.formula: VaR_alpha(X) = -inf{ x : F_X(x) > alpha } = F_Y^{-1}(1 - alpha), where X is P/L with distribution F_X and Y = -X is the loss; i.e. the (1 - alpha) quantile of the loss distribution.
concept.failure_modes: VaR says nothing about severity beyond the quantile — a 99% VaR is silent on whether the 1% day costs 1.1x or 50x VaR — and it is not subadditive, so a combined portfolio's VaR can exceed the sum of its parts. Normality assumptions, stale windows, and illiquid marks understate it in exactly the crises it is meant to capture.
concept.misconceptions: VaR is not the maximum you can lose: it marks the boundary of normal days, and institutions can and do lose multiples of it. A small VaR does not mean small risk when the tail beyond it is fat.
concept.example: A one-day 95% VaR of $1M means a loss of $1M or more is expected about one day in twenty; it is silent on whether that bad day loses $1.1M or $10M, which is what expected shortfall adds.
